sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Suillus variegatus is a bolete with a yellow-brown to olive cap, finely felted at first and later mottled with small darker scales. The tubes are short; pores are very small and crowded when young, then enlarge slightly and become olive to olive-brown. The stout yellowish to brownish stem has no ring. Lemon-yellow to orange-yellow flesh may blue weakly when cut; the smell is often acidic and sometimes described as chlorine-like.

sections.title: Habitat and caution
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species is associated mainly with pines, especially Pinus sylvestris and P. nigra. It grows in pinewoods, often on dry, poor sandy soils with variable pH. DGfM and VAPKO lists include it among recommended edible mushrooms, though culinary opinions are mixed. Caesium-137 levels depend strongly on location; follow local advisories. An entry cannot identify a collection reliably.

traits: Cap 5–15 cm across, yellow-brown to olive, finely felted at first then mottled with small darker scales; dry, sometimes slightly sticky in wet weather
Short tubes; pores very small, crowded and angular, yellow-olive to olive-brown with age, sometimes faintly blueing when bruised
Stout stem 4–12 cm tall, ochre-yellow to brownish, nearly smooth at maturity, without a ring or glandular dots
Lemon-yellow to orange-yellow flesh, sometimes weakly blueing when cut; acidic smell, sometimes described as chlorine-like
Ectomycorrhizal with pines, especially Pinus sylvestris and P. nigra; found in dry pinewoods and often on poor sandy soils, which may be acidic to basic
safetyNote: The DGfM and VAPKO list it among edible/recommended mushrooms, though its culinary value is often considered poor and its acidic or chlorine-like smell may be unpleasant. Like other wild mushrooms, it can accumulate caesium-137 in contaminated areas; levels depend strongly on the site. Consume mushrooms only after certain identification by a qualified person and follow local foraging advisories.
